Nothing ground breaking but makes sense... ​Why It Feels Artificial (and How It’s Supposed to Work)
​The Framing Flaw: By asking an open question rather than "How are you feeling about work/your projects today?", it invites non-work noise (taxes, outfits, deliveries).
​The Granularity Trap: Forcing you to attach clinical emotion tags to fleeting, low-stakes thoughts makes the process feel performative rather than genuine.
​Why Companies Still Use It: Aggregated at scale, these tools ignore the individual trivialities and look for macro trends. If 40% of a department suddenly selects Overwhelmed and Confused after a leadership announcement, HR spots a systemic issue—even if an individual employee was just annoyed by a traffic jam.

I would like to share some concerns about my current work situation. My intention is not to create conflict, but to have an honest conversation with someone while hoping it does not negatively affect my already fragile working relationship with Tammy.

One of my main concerns is the amount of scope creep that has happened since I joined. I was hired primarily for a business development and lead generation role. Today, I am handling high-level executive recruitment processes for three different organizations simultaneously. This includes marketing open positions, candidate sourcing, screening, interview coordination, document preparation, scheduling, communications, and managing the day-to-day operational workflow for each search. I also continue to manage RFP research and related business development work.

I'm able to handle this workload largely because I've designed automations, templates, and systems that make many of these processes efficient. However, these responsibilities are significantly different from my professional background and the role I originally accepted.

Another concern is compensation. Since I was hired, the Colombian peso has appreciated significantly against the U.S. dollar. Because I was paid in USD while living in Colombia, my effective income in local currency decreased by roughly 25%, substantially reducing my purchasing power. This loss of income, among other personal and professional reasons, ultimately contributed to my decision to relocate to Argentina. At the same time, my responsibilities have continued to expand, including absorbing many of the duties of a coworker who left the organization.

I also struggle with the lack of structure around my work. Goals are rarely defined for projects or recurring responsibilities. Most work is assigned through individual emails or text messages without measurable objectives, timelines, or success metrics. This makes it difficult to prioritize work or understand what success looks like.

Reporting is another source of frustration. I regularly prepare reports when requested, but I have never received meaningful feedback on them or guidance on how they could be improved. Likewise, I have never seen those reports used to evaluate results or support decision-making. Instead, conversations tend to focus on day-to-day operational issues or new requests rather than progress toward broader business goals.

Communication itself is often challenging. Nearly everything is managed through Gmail and text messages, even routine operational discussions that would be much easier to organize in project management or collaboration tools. Although I've introduced systems such as a CRM and proposed other tools to improve visibility and coordination, they have not been adopted. As a result, information is frequently scattered across long email threads, previous conversations are difficult to reference, and the same information often has to be shared multiple times.

The overall experience is frustrating because there is a constant sense that something is wrong, yet there is little discussion about improving the underlying processes that create those issues. I believe many of the daily frustrations could be reduced with clearer goals, defined workflows, and better communication systems.

I value the opportunity to contribute and have demonstrated that I can take on complex responsibilities. My hope is simply to have an honest conversation about whether my current responsibilities, compensation, and expectations are aligned, while ensuring that raising these concerns does not negatively affect my working relationship with Tammy.

I’ve been with the company for about two years, and one area I feel could be improved is scheduling and how server performance is evaluated.

I understand that PPA and LBW are important numbers, and I’ve been actively working to improve mine. However, I don’t think those two numbers alone always show a server’s overall performance. Different shifts can have completely different opportunities, especially with happy hour from 3–6, slower days, different sections, and comparing restaurant servers to the bar.

For example, a server could have a higher PPA or LBW while only doing around $800 in sales, while another server could generate $3,500 in sales and still receive fewer shifts because their percentages were lower. I feel total sales and overall contribution should also be considered.

I consistently upsell, take care of my side work, have strong relationships with regular customers, come in and help when coverage is needed, and I’ve been working on improving my voids. I also won an upselling competition here, so I feel I’ve shown that I care about performing well and contributing to the restaurant.

What has been frustrating is seeing hours and days being cut during slow season while new servers continue to be hired and, in some cases, receive more shifts. After being here for two years and consistently trying to contribute, it can make it feel like reliability, experience, and loyalty are not being taken into consideration.

I’m not asking for special treatment. I would just like scheduling to consider the full picture — PPA, LBW, total sales, guest service, reliability, experience, improvement, and overall contribution — rather than relying so heavily on only a couple of percentages. I believe having clearer and more balanced expectations would make scheduling feel fairer and give employees a better understanding of what they need to do to earn consistent hours.

I genuinely enjoy working here and take pride in my job. I understand that being here for two years doesn’t automatically entitle me to a perfect schedule or the busiest shifts. At the same time, I feel that consistency, reliability, work ethic, and loyalty should count for something. I’ve been here through some of our slowest seasons, including times when there were only a handful of us. I’ve consistently made myself available when the restaurant needed help, picked up shifts, worked on improving my numbers, and tried to go the extra mile for both the restaurant and our guests.

That’s why it can be discouraging during an already slow season to continue hiring additional servers while existing employees are being reduced to two or three shifts a week, sometimes only four hours at a time. It’s even harder to understand when newer employees are being scheduled on some of the highest-volume shifts, such as Fridays and Saturdays, while experienced employees are losing those opportunities.

I don’t have anything against our new employees, and everyone deserves an opportunity to work and succeed. My concern is whether we’re spreading the available hours too thin during a season when there already aren’t enough hours to go around.

We’ve also seen a similar cycle in the past where employees with very limited availability—sometimes only one or two days a week—were eventually let go because that availability didn’t meet the restaurant’s needs. Now it feels like we’re moving back toward having a larger staff again while some employees have very limited availability and others who are consistently available are receiving fewer shifts. I think it would be worth looking at whether continuing that cycle is beneficial for the restaurant or the employees.

There are employees here who have made this restaurant their primary job and have invested years into being dependable and building relationships with our regular guests. Some employees with other jobs may only be scheduled once a week and understandably may not be as dependent on that shift, while for others this is their primary source of income. I’m not saying people with second jobs should receive less simply because they have another job, but I do believe consistent availability, reliability, and commitment to this restaurant should be factors when hours are limited.

When hours become this inconsistent, it becomes difficult to know whether we’ll be able to make enough each week. I’m not saying any of this to bash the restaurant or management. I care about this place, which is exactly why I’m bringing it up.

I would just like to see a more consistent and transparent scheduling system that considers the full picture—overall performance, PPA/LBW, total sales, reliability, availability, experience, guest service, improvement, and consistent contribution to the restaurant.

I believe clearer expectations would benefit everyone. If there are specific standards we need to meet to earn more shifts or higher-volume shifts, I would appreciate knowing exactly what those expectations are so we have something clear and fair to work toward.
